summary: Modular monolith: React (Vite SPA) (web) on Go 1.27 (net/http + chi) with Azure Database for PostgreSQL – Flexible Server 17, hosted on Azure App Service — West Europe (Netherlands), at an estimated $484-2538/month.

frontend.justification: Rich interactive screens for a real-time collaboration app; team already writes typescript for the UI; good performance (priority 5/5); good scalability (priority 5/5).

alternatives.why_not: With priorities.time_to_market=3 (neutral), React is faster to deliver with.
Learning curve 3/5 for a senior team (team.experience=senior). Known limit of Next.js: server runtime needed for SSR; more moving parts than a static site.

tradeoffs: Client-rendered pages are weak for SEO
frontend.contrast: React (Vite SPA) (web) rather than Vue 3 (Vite SPA). With priorities.time_to_market=3 (neutral), React is faster to deliver with. Trade-off accepted: Client-rendered pages are weak for SEO.

backend.justification: Team already writes go for the API; native WebSocket support; good performance (priority 5/5); good scalability (priority 5/5).

alternatives.why_not: With priorities.performance=5 and priorities.security=3 (neutral), Go 1.27 is faster at runtime and stronger on security (close call). Known limit of Node.js 24 LTS + NestJS: more boilerplate than Express.
Team lists go, typescript but this needs csharp (team.languages=go,typescript).

tradeoffs: More hand-written code than batteries-included frameworks

pareto.note: No eligible option rates at least as well on all six priorities (cost, delivery, scalability, performance, maintainability, security).

confidence.label: low
confidence.basis: stability 0.59 (sensitive) over 54 priority vectors; score margin 0.8 over the runner-up (near-tie).

backend.contrast: Go 1.27 (net/http + chi) rather than Node.js 24 LTS + NestJS (TypeScript). With priorities.performance=5 and priorities.security=3 (neutral), Go 1.27 is faster at runtime and stronger on security (close call). Trade-off accepted: More hand-written code than batteries-included frameworks.

database.choice: Azure Database for PostgreSQL – Flexible Server 17 — West Europe (Netherlands)
database.justification: Strict ACID transactions for payments and the records they change; row-level security enforces tenant isolation in the database; handles write-heavy load; good maintainability (priority 4/5); good performance (priority 5/5).

alternatives.why_not: With priorities.maintainability=4 and priorities.security=3 (neutral), Azure Database for PostgreSQL – Flexible Server 17 is easier to maintain and stronger on security.

With priorities.maintainability=4, Azure Database for PostgreSQL – Flexible Server 17 is easier to maintain; it fits better: strict ACID transactions for payments and the records they change (requirements.payments=true).

tradeoffs: Vertical write scaling; sharding needs extensions

confidence.label: high
confidence.basis: stability 1.00 (robust) over 54 priority vectors; score margin 3.2 over the runner-up.

database.contrast: Azure Database for PostgreSQL – Flexible Server 17 rather than Supabase Postgres. With priorities.maintainability=4 and priorities.security=3 (neutral), Azure Database for PostgreSQL – Flexible Server 17 is easier to maintain and stronger on security. Trade-off accepted: Vertical write scaling; sharding needs extensions.

hosting.choice: Azure App Service (Linux, Premium v3, 2+ instances) — West Europe (Netherlands)
hosting.justification: Good maintainability (priority 4/5); good performance (priority 5/5); deployment slots for safe releases. Satisfies the hard constraints (managed_cloud (no servers to patch)).

alternatives.why_not: With priorities.maintainability=4 and priorities.time_to_market=3 (neutral), Azure App Service is easier to maintain and faster to deliver with. Known limit of Google Cloud Run: cold starts unless min instances are paid for.
With priorities.maintainability=4 and priorities.time_to_market=3 (neutral), Azure App Service is easier to maintain and faster to deliver with.

tradeoffs: Less control than containers for unusual runtimes

what_would_change.new_choice: AWS Elastic Beanstalk (managed platform on EC2) — eu-central-1 (Frankfurt)

supporting.choice: Keycloak 26 (container next to the API) with Google OAuth
supporting.justification: social login on a self-hosted identity server: Go has no batteries-included auth framework, so Keycloak handles passwords, MFA and social providers and keeps identities in-region.

alternatives.why_not: per-active-user pricing across ~50,000 users and identity data outside the EU
security-sensitive code the team would have to maintain

supporting.justification: ~200 GB of files in 12 months: uploads (images, documents) go straight from clients to object storage via signed URLs. Private bucket, server-generated signed URLs, encryption with managed keys.

alternatives.why_not: with ~200 GB of data expected in 12 months (scale.data_volume_gb_12_months), files inside the database bloat every backup and cost more per GB than object storage
zero egress fees, but a second vendor outside Azure

supporting.choice: Yjs CRDT documents + Hocuspocus WebSocket server
supporting.justification: Several people edit the same shared item at once (description evidence): CRDTs merge concurrent edits without conflicts and broadcast cursors/presence (awareness); Hocuspocus persists document updates to the database. The knowledge base has no Yjs-compatible server for Go 1.27, so Hocuspocus runs as a separate Node.js service.

alternatives.why_not: fastest to start but per-room pricing and the shared data held by a third party
last-write-wins loses concurrent edits

alternatives.choice: A sync server in the backend's language
alternatives.why_not: no Yjs-compatible server for it in the knowledge base

tradeoffs: An extra Node.js runtime beside Go 1.27: its own deploys, dependency updates and monitoring; it must verify the API's auth tokens
Stateful socket servers need sticky routing or a Redis pub/sub backplane when scaled out

supporting.choice: Azure Managed Redis in West Europe (Netherlands)
supporting.justification: ~5,000 concurrent users would otherwise send every lookup to the database; pub/sub backplane so WebSocket messages reach users on every instance; performance priority 5 (cache and pub/sub layer).

alternatives.why_not: 7.4-7.8 are source-available (RSALv2/SSPLv1) and Redis 8+ adds an AGPLv3 option (copyleft for network use); Valkey keeps the BSD licence
being retired (Sept 2028); Azure Managed Redis is the replacement

tradeoffs: Another stateful component to size and monitor

supporting.choice: Azure Service Bus in West Europe (Netherlands)
supporting.justification: Payment-gateway webhooks at ~50,000 users processed idempotently with retries; absorbs write bursts, so none of it blocks a request.

alternatives.why_not: a slow or failed call would lose or double-apply a payment event

supporting.choice: Stripe (Checkout) — Stripe Billing with per-seat subscription quantities
supporting.justification: Taking payments for a real-time collaboration app (requirements.payments) through hosted checkout keeps card data off your servers, which can qualify for PCI DSS SAQ A (your acquirer confirms; protect the checkout page from script attacks). Payment confirmation is trusted only from signed server-side webhooks.

alternatives.why_not: handles global tax but higher fees and less control
enterprise pricing and onboarding for ~50,000 users

tradeoffs: Per-transaction fees (~2% domestic cards) are charged on revenue, not in the infrastructure band

supporting.justification: At ~50,000 users, public pages and static assets are cached near users so the origin serves less traffic; only public, non-personal content is cached.

alternatives.why_not: every asset request from the 50,000 expected users would hit the origin, adding latency and origin load

alternatives.choice: Cloudflare (free plan) in front of Azure
alternatives.why_not: cheaper for a small site, but a second vendor for DNS/TLS and outside the Azure contract

tradeoffs: Front Door Standard has a $35/month base fee before requests and egress

supporting.justification: Go 1.27 tests run on every push and a passing build deploys to Azure App Service; the cost band reserves $0-20/month for a team of 5 (planning estimate).

alternatives.why_not: equally capable; for a team of 5 with a DevOps engineer (team.has_devops=true), ready-made GitHub deploy actions for Azure App Service mean less pipeline code to maintain

tradeoffs: Secrets must be stored as encrypted environment secrets

supporting.choice: Azure Monitor + Application Insights in West Europe (Netherlands)
supporting.justification: The 100 ms p95 target and the 99.9% availability target are watched by latency and error-rate alerts; logs and metrics stay with Azure in West Europe (Netherlands), so there is no second vendor.

alternatives.why_not: an extra vendor account for a team of 5; Azure Monitor + Application Insights in West Europe already covers 99.9% availability alerting, add Sentry later for richer error grouping

tradeoffs: Log retention costs grow with traffic

supporting.choice: Tenant isolation: tenant_id on every row + database row-level security
supporting.justification: Several customer organisations share one real-time collaboration app: every query is scoped by tenant, enforced in the database, so one bug cannot leak another organisation's data.

alternatives.why_not: strong isolation, but a separate database to provision, migrate and back up per customer organisation, for a team of 5

tradeoffs: Every new table needs a policy

assumptions: Hosting Azure App Service (Linux, Premium v3, 2+ instances): $150-800/month at the 'medium' tier.
Database Azure Database for PostgreSQL – Flexible Server 17: $150-700/month.

auth: Keycloak 26 (container next to the API) with Google OAuth runs as another app on the same Azure App Service (Linux, Premium v3, 2+ instances) plan: $0-0/month extra; size the plan's memory for it.
realtime: Yjs CRDT documents + Hocuspocus WebSocket server $25-150/month. Basis: one extra small always-on instance for the Node.js sync server at the host's entry price (estimate).
cache: Azure Managed Redis in West Europe (Netherlands) $60-350/month.
queue: Azure Service Bus in West Europe (Netherlands) $5-30/month.
observability: Azure Monitor + Application Insights in West Europe (Netherlands) $30-200/month.

Stored data ~200 GB after 12 months at ~$0.02-0.035/GB-month: $4-8/month (year-end volume used as an upper bound, not an average); bulk files and media are assumed to sit in object storage, while database rows stay small.
Spiky traffic: the upper bound is a peak month; with autoscaling, quiet months run near the lower bound.
Excluded: payment gateway fees (~2% per transaction) are a share of revenue, not infrastructure.
Excluded: taxes, domain names, paid support plans and data-egress spikes. Order-of-magnitude band, not a quote.

warnings.message: p95 100 ms is achievable only with users near the Azure App Service (Linux, Premium v3, 2+ instances) region and no cross-region calls; the engine cannot measure it — load-test before launch.

GDPR: lawful basis and privacy notice, data-subject rights endpoints, DPAs with every processor (Art. 28), security of processing (Art. 32); transfers outside the EU need an adequacy decision or SCCs.

Upper estimate $2538/month is 69% above the $1500 budget at peak usage; the largest upper-bound items are Hosting Azure App Service (Linux, Premium v3, 2+ instances) (up to $800) and Database Azure Database for PostgreSQL – Flexible Server 17 (up to $700). Launch near the $484 lower bound and set billing alerts at the budget.

assumptions: Knowledge base as of 2026-11-11; lifecycle and pricing judgements use that date, not the run date.
Scale tier 'medium' from 50,000 users and ~5,000 peak concurrent users (people, not requests per second; used only for sizing and cost).
gdpr with no data_residency: EU region (West Europe (Netherlands)) chosen to avoid international transfers.
